extracted.intended_audience: mathematics instructors (undergraduate and graduate), course designers, and educators interested in assessment practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and implementing formative and summative assessment practices in mathematics courses, including peer/self-assessment routines (PAR), portfolios, projects, multimodal assignments, rubrics, and alternatives to traditional exams and grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-assessment components
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-assessment is a complex and iterative process that includes several interrelated steps: understanding learning criteria, gathering feedback, and reflecting on one’s skills relative to the feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To learn to effectively self-assess, students need proficiency with each component skill (e.g., judging which feedback is useful). These 'feedback literacies' can be tied back to steps of the assessment cycle and should be explicitly taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize Dunning–Kruger as a barrier to self-assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: People who are struggling are often unable to recognize their own struggles (Dunning–Kruger effect), while more advanced students better see their limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should account for this double-bind when assigning self-assessment tasks and teach the component skills of assessment so struggling students can better judge their understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-Assisted Reflection (PAR) routine
rubrics_metrics.description: A structured routine for peer feedback consisting of: 1) Write up a draft solution, 2) reflect on the draft, 3) exchange peer feedback, and 4) revise and turn in the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PAR has been used across contexts (intro calculus to graduate analysis), increased passing rates in studies, and should be incorporated regularly (weekly recommended) to build feedback literacies. PAR packets organize the cycle and the turned-in packet should include received feedback and revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAR packet components
rubrics_metrics.description: A PAR packet consists of a cover page (with the homework prompt), a place for an initial draft, a place for reflection, a place for peer feedback, and additional space to write up a revised solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide students a template (physical or LaTeX) so they submit their draft, reflections, peer comments, and revision together; this documents the feedback cycle and supports accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAR logistics and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Designate one short class meeting ('PAR day')—about 15 minutes—where students bring drafts, pair randomly, silently read for ~5 minutes, then discuss/provide feedback for ~5–10 minutes, and later revise and submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekly repetition helps students overcome the initial learning curve; enforce silent reading first (no clarifying questions) so students focus on interpreting written work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting PAR problems: low floor, high ceiling, multiple approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose problems that everyone can at least start (low floor) but few can finish correctly on first try (high ceiling); problems with multiple solutions or that require explanation/justification are especially productive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features create space for peers to bring different approaches, compare and contrast, and deepen conceptual understanding—ideal for PAR activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial draft expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should produce an initial attempt that conveys their reasoning, choices, and where they struggled so peers can give meaningful feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems should encourage students to commit to a method (e.g., devise and explain approximation method before calculations), enabling substantive peer critique rather than mere correctness checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reflection prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explicit reflection prompts students complete after drafting (examples provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample prompts: 1) Did you show all steps? 2) Did you explain why, not just what? 3) Did you avoid use of ambiguous pronouns? 4) Did you define all variables? 5) Did you provide appropriate diagrams, figures, graphs, etc.? 6) Did you verify if your solution is reasonable? These prompts both scaffold student reflection and guide peer feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer feedback procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Students read a peer solution, write comments, then discuss; the process is fluid and can include clarifying discussion, comparison of approaches, or collaborative problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage written comments followed by conversation. Examples show peers bounding approximations from above and below to improve error estimates—peer approaches can interact productively to reveal better methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision as a required step
rubrics_metrics.description: After peer feedback and conferences, students must revise their work and submit the revised solution as part of the PAR packet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision is critical to ensure feedback is incorporated into learning (not just received and forgotten). Revisions may be informed by peer discussions, class/instructor conversations, or further reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing feedback literacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Create activities to help students learn to provide and use feedback effectively, positioning them as active agents rather than only recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include presenting small samples of written work (preferably familiar problem contexts), asking students to assess individually then discuss as a class, and comparing samples to an external rubric or standard to build evaluative judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darts classification activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A quick classification scheme for sample solutions: 'bullseye' (correct explanation), 'on the board' (mostly correct but communicated poorly or minor error), and 'off the mark' (incorrect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a warm-up or entry task to practice evaluative judgment and to seed class discussion about quality differences in solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic summative assessments principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Summative assessments should describe what students have learned in authentic, inclusive, and collaborative ways rather than solely reproducing high-stakes, inauthentic exams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View summative assessment as something done with students (co-creation), incorporate universal design principles and choices to empower marginalized students, and favor assessments that let students demonstrate learning in meaningful contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolios as alternatives to final exams
rubrics_metrics.description: Use portfolios to showcase student learning over the semester with checkpoints during the term; portfolios may be physical or electronic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample portfolio contents: cover letter (1–2 pages reflecting on learning), table of contents, math biography, selected portfolio items (10 proofs/problems highlighted), in-class activities, PAR homework assignments, and essays. For each portfolio item include a short 'portfolio card' describing the item and why it was chosen. Electronic portfolios enable multimodality and easier checkpoints/feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project design for authentic assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects should be substantive, longer-term engagements that offer student agency, multiple options, scaffolding, and opportunities for feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects are especially natural in applied contexts (data analysis, modeling) but are feasible in pure math with creativity. Plan group roles, responsibilities, community agreements, check-ins, and assessment practices. Consider industry/community partnerships and require accessible deliverables (technical report or presentation for stakeholders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Students as teachers (teaching as assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Position students to teach peers as a learning and assessment activity, which consolidates their thinking and reveals understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer positioning students as instructors (expert role) over high-pressure public evaluation; alternatives include recorded digital presentations, poster sessions, or formal talks depending on learning goals and necessary scaffolding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal essays and alternative communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use essays and multimodal outputs (websites, blog posts, Wikipedia articles, mixed media) to develop epistemologies of mathematics and technical communication skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear assessment criteria (rubrics, learning goals, discussions) so students know expectations. Multimodal outputs can increase audience and engagement and build digital literacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and co-creation of rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubrics clarify learning goals and describe continua of skill (e.g., emerging to higher levels) so students can gauge progress and direct learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involve students in generating rubrics (co-creation) to build assessment literacy and agency. Align rubrics with targeted assessments for better feedback and instruction design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable exam practices and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: If exams are used, make them more equitable by reducing time pressure and stereotype threat (e.g., use take-home exams, allow resources, permit group exams, and offer exam corrections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timed, high-stakes in-person exams limit access and authenticity; consider alternatives that reduce stress and better measure meaningful learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative grading approach: decouple feedback from grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide many opportunities for assessment and feedback that aren’t tied to grades; carefully choose what to grade and how, because grading can reduce learning and motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research shows written feedback without a grade outperforms grades (d = 1.14 pooled) and comments alone increase intrinsic motivation (d = 1.60). Combining grades with comments can eliminate the benefits of written feedback. Use ungraded formative activities widely and be deliberate about summative grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitfalls and limits of grades as measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Grades typically conflate multiple factors (performance, learning, effort, attendance, participation, privilege, test-taking ability, peer comparison, noise) and lack a standard meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that grades are an imperfect, noisy proxy for learning and can reproduce inequities (racial/gender biases, language demands); this should motivate more authentic and inclusive assessment practices.
